newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Markets wary of NZ election, scramble to square up.
newsitem.headline: Markets wary of NZ election, scramble to square up.

text.p: New Zealand's financial markets were scrambling to establish neutral to short positions ahead of Saturday's general election, acknowledging that the outcome was too close to call, analysts said on Friday.
"In terms of where the market is at the moment, the expectations are leading more towards a change of government after the election," said David Drage, ANZ Bank Treasury Economist.
"But overriding that completely is the fact that there's just so much uncertainty about what the new voting system could kick up."
New Zealanders usher in a new era in the country's history on Saturday, voting for the first time under a system of proportional representation likely to produce a minority or coalition government.
The Labour opposition has made a strong finish to its campaign and polls suggest the centre-left parties between them have the numbers to oust the conservative National Party from power.
But the markets have had their fingers burnt by elections before, particularly in 1993, and traders said discretion was proving the better part of valour this time around.
"Last election people took positions and they got creamed because the polls suggested it was going to be a one horse race," a bond dealer observed.
The 1993 election instead resulted in a hung parliament, National gaining a slim majority only after special votes had been counted ten days after the election.
"No one wants to take that punt again," the dealer said.
In recent weeks the markets have surprised many, shrugging off political uncertainty in favour of a bull run.
The share market posted a 2-1/2 year high on Monday while the currency was at an eight-year high just two weeks ago.

But in the final days before the election, investors have looked to square up their positions, the currency falling about 70 basis points against the U.S. dollar and the ten-year bond yield rising above eight percent.
"It's trying to square up, it's having trouble squaring up," one dealer said of the debt market. "There seems to be quite a bit of panic out there today."

Another said Helen Clark had led the Labour party to a stronger position than many had anticipated. Her wins in all the leaders' debates have seen Labour surge in opinion polls to within about four percentage points of National.
"Really it's down to the wire now," the dealer said. "Helen Clark is doing way too well for the financial markets and they're spitting the dummy a bit."
However, trade was thin in all markets and any desperate last minute realignments would pale in comparison with the volatility expected next week.
"I expect Monday to be frantic with the (bond) market gapping all over the place," one trader said. "It will take a little while to settle down too."
Few expect a clear-cut result on election night and coalition talks between the main parties could drag on for weeks after the election.
"If we end up with a National-led majority or minority government next week, expect to see all rates down by about 25 to 30 basis points and the currency way up," the dealer said.
A currency trader concurred, saying a National victory would see the Kiwi rise rapidly above 70 U.S. cents.
But if the election resulted in a Labour-led government, dealers said rates would fall by about the same amount and the Kiwi would pull back, though not to an alarming degree.
